title: Cellulitis, Necrotizing Fasciitis, and Subcutaneous Infections

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man presented with a painful swelling on his thigh. He denied any associated fevers or chills. The patient had applied warm compresses to the site for the past two days with little improvement. He was normally well and did not take any regular medication. On examination, there was a 3-cm lesion on his right inner thigh. The lesion was warm, tender, and fluctuant to palpation. The rest of his physical examination was unremarkable.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Hold antibiotics pending results of a superficial swab MCS
Incision and drainage at the bedside
List for urgent surgical debridement in an operating room

questions.explanation: Incision and drainage at the bedside A carbuncle of this size is likely to respond well to bedside incision and drainage. Antibiotics alone are unlikely to address the infection, and surgical debridement of the carbuncle and/or hospitalization to receive intravenous antibiotics for a lesion of this size is not indicated, particularly given that the patient does not have any systemic signs of infection (e.g., fevers, chills). Superficial skin cultures are likely to grow commensal flora; abscess cultures are preferred to guide antibiotic therapy.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q23

questions.stem: A 56-year-old woman presented with a 2-week history of fevers and painful skin nodules. She had a past medical history of immune neutropenia. On examination, her temperature was 38.8 oC, her blood pressure was 136/72 mmHg, her heart rate was 78 beats/minute, and her respiratory rate was 14 breaths/minute. There were several tender nodules over her forearms and dorsum of hands. The nodules were 1–2 cm in diameter and had a violaceous discoloration. Investigations: Total white cell count 46 ×109/L
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Sweet syndrome This patient with immune neutropenia is likely on granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) as her WBC count is very elevated. Sweet syndrome is the typical cause of painful nodules in a patient on G-CSF .
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q45

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man presented with increasing left lower extremity pain and swelling at the site of a minor trauma sustained 5 days prior. He had a history of bipolar affective disorder, alcohol abuse, and no drug allergies. On examination, significant induration and erythema were noted, along with a temperature of 38.5°C and a white blood cell count of 18,000/mm3. Broad-spectrum antimicrobial treatment was started with meropenem 1 gram IV q8hours. He was taken to the operating room, where necrotizing fascia and purulence were noted in the distal extremity. Cultures of multiple intraoperative specimens were positive for Streptococcus pyogenes. Antibiotic therapy was subsequently changed to penicillin G 4 million units IV q4 hours.
questions.lead_in: What agent would be most appropriate to add to penicillin to help control the pathogenicity of this infection?
questions.explanation: Clindamycin Adding clindamycin introduces a 2nd agent with an alternative mechanism of action. Clindamycin acts on the ribosome, interrupting protein synthesis, and hence toxin production. IDSA recommend that dual therapy with penicillin and clindamycin is used for S. pyogenes necrotising fasciitis. Doxycycline does not provide adequate coverage of Streptococcus pyogenes and would not be indicated in this case. Since S. pyogenes are reliably sensitive to penicillin, gentamicin would not be expected to help control pathogenicity of this infection. There is no evidence of an anaerobic component to this infection, making the addition of metronidazole unnecessary. Penicillin G is considered to be the most active antibiotic against S. pyogenes. The addition of vancomycin would not be expected to further control the pathogenicity of this infection, given the fact that there is no evidence of beta-lactam-resistant organisms in this case.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q5

questions.stem: A 42-year-old man was reviewed with new onset pustular lesions spreading through the legs, arms, and abdomen. He was on day 6 vancomycin and day 2 piperacillin/tazobactam for a right leg cellulitis which was slow to respond (top image). He had a history of chronic lymphedema due to obstructive sleep apnea with secondary pulmonary hypertension. On examination the patient was well, his blood pressure was 138/72 mmHg, his heart rate was 92 beats/minute, and his temperature was 38.4°C. There were widespread skin lesions (bottom image). Investigations: Total white cell count 15 ×109/L Absolute neutrophil count 13.2 ×109/L
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP) Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP) is an eruption commonly related to drugs (90%). Commonly associated drugs include antibiotics (penicillins and other beta-lactams commonly) as well as calcium channel blockers and other drugs. This pattern has also been reported postviral illness (e.g., enterovirus, adenovirus, EBV , CMV , HBV , etc.). Typically there is an acute onset after drug exposure (within 1–2 days), and the rash starts with pustules on an erythematous base (often begin on face or intertriginous areas), accompanied by fever and neutrophilia (due to IL-8 secretion by T cells and keratinocytes). Symptoms resolve with discontinuation of the offending drug, and skin will desquamate in the subsequent 4-10 days.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q47

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman presented with a 4-day history of worsening pain and swelling of her right arm. She had a history of hypertension, atrial fibrillation, and diet-controlled diabetes. She had a radical mastectomy and chemotherapy for invasive breast cancer 5 years prior, with an associated DVT of her right leg; and was currently undergoing investigation for unexplained iron-deficiency anemia.
questions.lead_in: What risk factor is most likely to be responsible for her current infection?
questions.explanation: Chronic lymphedema postsurgery All of the options (skin barrier disruption or inflammation, immunosuppression, preexisting skin infections, and edema) can be risk factors for the development of cellulitis. However, in this particular instance, it is her arm that is affected, and the risk of lymphedema following axillary node dissection (ANC) and radiotherapy for breast cancer is high (roughly 40% if both ANC and radiotherapy). Onset of lymphedema is insidious and progressive. Patients with lymphedema have an increased risk of infection in the affected area (up to 70×); over a quarter of patients will have at least one infection annually.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q28

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man presented with a foul-smelling right lower extremity soft tissue infection. He was obese and had a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, anemia, hyperlipidemia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and a recent deep vein thrombosis. He had no known drug allergies. Home medications were ferrous sulfate 325 mg PO TD, tizanidine 2 mg PO BD, theophylline 300 mg PO BD, warfarin 5 mg PO daily, and atorvastatin 40 mg PO daily. On examination, he was afebrile with an infected ulcer on his right lower leg. Investigations: Total white cell count 9800 cells/mm3 MRI: no evidence of underlying osteomyelitis Wound swab culture: mixed organisms including Pseudomonas isolated Plans were to treat the infection with ciprofloxacin PO and amoxicillin-clavulanic acid PO.
questions.lead_in: What medication would be most likely to interfere with the effectiveness of this planned antibiotic regimen?
questions.explanation: Ferrous sulfate Atorvastatin would not be expected to interact with the planned antibiotic regimen. Ciprofloxacin can significantly increase serum concentrations of theophylline, tizanidine, and warfarin and should be avoided in combination with these agents. Polyvalent metallic cations, such as ferrous sulfate, can adsorb oral fluoroquinolone doses and dramatically reduce systemic exposure and clinical effects of the fluoroquinolone.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q5

questions.question: 18. 55-year old male who had a saphenectomy several years ago. He's had several (3-4 per year) episodes of swelling and cellulitis for the past few years. He comes back with a recurrence of this problem.

parts.text: What is the most likely pathogen?
b) Name 2 important interventions to reduce his risk of recurrence

cohort_answer.text: Pathogen: GAS. Interventions: Compression stocking to reduce edema; Suppressive antibiotics e.g. penicillin/cephalexin; Ensure good foot care (treat dermatophyte infection, moisturize to prevent cracks); Treating fungal foot infections if present.

questions.question: A man underwent CABG with saphenous vein harvest. He has frequent episodes of redness and swelling in his leg. A picture of cellulitis around saphenous harvest site is given.

parts.text: Name the most likely organism.
Name three different strategies to reduce frequency of infections in this patient.

questions.model_answer:
a) Most likely organism: a non-group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus (group C, G, or B streptococcus) - the classic cause of recurrent cellulitis at a saphenous vein harvest site.
b) Three strategies to reduce recurrence: (1) Treat/prevent interdigital tinea pedis, the usual portal of entry. (2) Use graduated compression stockings and maintain good skin hygiene/limb elevation to reduce chronic lymphedema and venous insufficiency. (3) If episodes remain frequent despite the above, initiate prophylactic antibiotics (e.g., monthly benzathine penicillin or oral penicillin V twice daily, or a macrolide if penicillin-allergic).

parts.text: Cellulitis

VAP

questions.model_answer: Shortest recommended durations: Cellulitis - 5 days; Acute uncomplicated pyelonephritis - 5-7 days (e.g., with a fluoroquinolone); Peritonsillar abscess (comparable to adult CAP context) - 5-7 days after drainage; Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) - 7 days; Frontal (bacterial) brain abscess - typically 4-6 weeks of IV therapy (shortest end of the accepted range), longer than the other listed infections given the difficulty of source control and CNS penetration requirements.

questions.question: 20. Nec fasc of arm

parts.text: How do you make the diagnosis of nec fasc
What empiric antimicrobial regimen do you use
What IPC precautions do you need
Sibling is pen allergic (anaphylaxis) name 2 other drugs you can use for prophylaxis

questions.model_answer:
a) Necrotizing fasciitis is confirmed by immediate surgical exploration - the gold standard: gray/dishwater fluid, non-bleeding and non-contracting fascia/muscle, and easy separation of fascia from subcutaneous tissue with blunt dissection (positive finger test); frozen-section biopsy and Gram stain of exudate can support intraoperative diagnosis. Adjuncts such as CT/MRI (soft tissue gas or fascial edema) or the LRINEC score can raise suspicion preoperatively but should never delay surgical exploration.
b) Empiric regimen: vancomycin (or linezolid, to cover MRSA) PLUS piperacillin-tazobactam or a carbapenem (e.g., meropenem, to cover streptococci, Enterobacteriaceae, and anaerobes) PLUS clindamycin (to suppress toxin/exotoxin production if group A Streptococcus is implicated).
c) Contact precautions should be applied given the possibility of MRSA; if group A Streptococcus (invasive GAS) is suspected or confirmed, droplet precautions should also be instituted until the patient has completed at least 24 hours of effective antimicrobial therapy.
d) For post-exposure prophylaxis of a close contact in a patient with penicillin anaphylaxis, two agents from different classes: clindamycin (lincosamide) and azithromycin (macrolide) - avoiding all beta-lactams, including cephalosporins, given the anaphylactic history.

questions.question: A 45-M is status post saphenous vein stripping for a CABG and presents with the 4th episode of cellulitis in the same leg.

parts.text: List 2 guideline proven strategies to prevent future occurrences

questions.model_answer: Guideline-proven strategies to prevent recurrent saphenous-vein-harvest-site cellulitis: (1) Prompt treatment/prevention of interdigital tinea pedis (the usual portal of entry). (2) Use of graduated compression stockings and good skin/limb hygiene to reduce chronic lymphedema/venous insufficiency (with lymphatic pneumatic compression for refractory lymphedema); prophylactic penicillin (e.g., monthly benzathine penicillin or oral penicillin V) can be added for patients with frequent recurrences despite these measures.

questions.question: Patient post aortocoronary bypass who had saphenous vein graft. Recurrent swelling and episodes of cellulitis of that leg.

parts.text: Why is it swollen?
What is the organism causing cellulitis?
What are 2 things you can tell him to reduce risk?

cohort_answer.text: Swelling due to decreased venous and lymphatic drainage and break of skin (reduced lymphatic drainage, venous insufficiency, surgical site collection). Organism: beta-hemolytic streptococcus (Group A, B, C, G most common); Group C streptococci classically isolated post vein harvest; route of entry often tinea pedis. Reduce risk: Compression/support stockings, good skin hygiene, treatment of tinea pedis, chemoprophylaxis if frequent recurrences (penicillin V 250-500mg PO BID x1 year, per PATCH-1 study)

questions.question: Patient who has a MRSA skin infection. And who has never had C. diff

parts.text: What is the most effective oral treatment that causes the least diarrhea in C. diff?
What is the most effective oral treatment that causes the most C. diff diarrhea?
What are two other factors in the treatment of this patient that have an impact on the development of C. diff diarrhea?
What are 2 antimicrobial measures to limit c diff risk?

cohort_answer.text:
Most effective oral treatment causing least diarrhea: Tetracyclines (also macrolides, narrow spectrum beta lactams)
Most effective oral treatment causing most C. diff diarrhea: Clindamycin
Two other factors: Advanced age; Duration of hospitalization; Prolonged exposure to antibiotics
Two antimicrobial measures to limit C diff risk: Minimize the frequency and duration of high-risk antibiotic therapy and the number of antibiotic agents prescribed, to reduce CDI risk (strong recommendation, moderate quality of evidence). Implement an antibiotic stewardship program (good practice recommendation). Antibiotics to be targeted should be based on the local epidemiology and the C. difficile strains present. Restriction of fluoroquinolones, clindamycin, and cephalosporins (except for surgical antibiotic prophylaxis) should be considered (strong recommendation, moderate quality of evidence). No evidence for d/c PPI or probiotics

questions.question: Patient traveled to India, presents scrotal edema with inflammation of the lymphatic path of a lower limb.

parts.text: What is the most likely organism
What is the mechanism for explaining edema
Name three diagnostic tests
He develops cellulitis of the lower limb, which organism is most likely involved?
Name 3 ways to prevent cellulitis in this patient

cohort_answer.text:
Most likely organism: Wuchereria bancrofti
Mechanism for edema: Redbook: Adult worms cause lymphatic dilatation and dysfunction, which result in abnormal lymph flow and eventually may lead to lymphedema in the legs, scrotal area (for W bancrofti only), and arms.
Three diagnostic tests: Circulating filarial antigen assay; Blood smears (10pm-4am); PCR; Serology; Ultrasound and lymphoscintigraphic techniques
Organism for cellulitis: Streptococcus pyogenes. Dx: Acute Dermato-Lymphangio-Adenitis (ADLA). Attacks of ADLA are characterised by localized pain and tenderness, lymphadenitis and/or lymphangitis and/or cellulitis and local warmth, with (mostly 97% cases) or without systemic manifestations of fever, nausea and vomiting. Secondary infections due to bacteria like Group A streptococcus are responsible.
Three ways to prevent cellulitis: Control of edema/promotion of lymph flow; Rigorous hygiene/foot care; Good glycaemic control if diabetic; Long term antibiotics ("In patients with advanced stages of lymphedema, proper local care of the limb is not always possible due to deep skin folds or warty projections. If such patients have recurrent (=>2 episodes) ADLA attacks, long-term antibiotic therapy using oral penicillin or long acting benzathine penicillin 1.2 MU, deep IM every 3 weeks is indicated")

questions.question: 40yo M, hx IVDU, recently incarcerated seen at OPAT with purulent cellulitis of R leg.

parts.text: What are the most common organisms causing this condition - give 2?

On further questioning he says he was at the beach and cut his foot on a shell before the infection started. You want to cover Vibrio vulnificus but are concerned about compliance. Give an oral antibiotic option for monotherapy to cover the pathogens of concern.
There were adverse effects related to the oral monotherapy you gave - give two regimens (IV +/- PO) that are alternatives. PO can be given max BID, IV max once daily.
Name 5 other organisms that can cause marine associated SSTIs

questions.model_answer:
a) 2 most common organisms causing purulent cellulitis in this context (IVDU): Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA) and Streptococcus pyogenes (group A Streptococcus).
b) Oral monotherapy option covering Vibrio vulnificus: doxycycline (has activity against Vibrio vulnificus as well as reasonable MRSA coverage).
c) 2 alternative regimens (IV +/- PO, PO max BID, IV max once daily): (1) ceftriaxone IV once daily + ciprofloxacin PO BID; (2) cefotaxime IV once daily + levofloxacin PO once daily.
d) 5 other organisms causing marine-associated SSTIs: Aeromonas hydrophila, Mycobacterium marinum, Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae, Vibrio alginolyticus, Vibrio parahaemolyticus (Shewanella algae also acceptable).

questions.question: Young person who comes in with hip pain out of proportion and hypotension. You suspect necrotizing fasciitis

parts.text: How can this diagnosis be confirmed?
Devise an empiric regimen for the person
Intra-operative sample gram stain shows gram positive cocci in chains, what if any isolation requirements are required?
You learn he was in contact with his mom who is anaphylactic to penicillin. List antibiotics from 2 different classes that can be used for prophylaxis (assuming susceptibility)

questions.model_answer:
a) Necrotizing fasciitis is confirmed by immediate surgical exploration - the gold standard: gray/dishwater fluid, non-bleeding and non-contracting fascia/muscle, and easy separation of fascia from subcutaneous tissue with blunt dissection (positive finger test); frozen-section biopsy and Gram stain of exudate can support intraoperative diagnosis. Adjuncts such as CT/MRI (soft tissue gas or fascial edema) or the LRINEC score can raise suspicion preoperatively but should never delay surgical exploration.
b) Empiric regimen: vancomycin (or linezolid, to cover MRSA) PLUS piperacillin-tazobactam or a carbapenem (e.g., meropenem, to cover streptococci, Enterobacteriaceae, and anaerobes) PLUS clindamycin (to suppress toxin/exotoxin production if group A Streptococcus is implicated).
c) Gram-positive cocci in chains on intraoperative Gram stain suggests group A Streptococcus (S. pyogenes); given this, droplet precautions should be added to contact precautions until the patient has received at least 24 hours of effective antimicrobial therapy.
d) For post-exposure prophylaxis of a close contact in a patient with penicillin anaphylaxis, two agents from different classes: clindamycin (lincosamide) and azithromycin (macrolide) - avoiding all beta-lactams, including cephalosporins, given the anaphylactic history.

questions.question: Purulent cellulitis in homeless individual.

parts.text: Name the two most likely pathogens to cause this
Tells you he cut it in sea water concerning for vibrio vulnificus, what empiric oral agent could cover all 3 organisms?
He gets allergy to that agent, design two regimens with a single daily IV and/or BID oral that could be used instead of above.
Name 5 organisms (genus and species) of acute water SSTI.

questions.model_answer:
a) The two most likely pathogens causing purulent cellulitis in this population: Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA) and Streptococcus pyogenes (group A Streptococcus).
b) Doxycycline is a reasonable single empiric oral agent providing activity against MRSA, streptococci, and Vibrio vulnificus.
c) Two alternative regimens (single daily-dose IV and/or twice-daily oral, maximum two drugs each): Regimen 1 - ceftriaxone 1-2 g IV once daily (covers Streptococcus and Vibrio) plus trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole PO twice daily (covers MRSA). Regimen 2 - ertapenem 1 g IV once daily (covers Streptococcus, Vibrio, and other gram-negatives) plus linezolid PO/IV 600 mg twice daily (covers MRSA and Streptococcus).
d) Five organisms causing acute water-associated skin/soft tissue infection: Vibrio vulnificus, Aeromonas hydrophila, Mycobacterium marinum, Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae, and Edwardsiella tarda.

questions.question: He presents with L leg swelling, erythema, pain 2 years later

parts.text: What is the likely cause

questions.model_answer:
a) Likely cause: recurrent cellulitis at the site of saphenous vein harvest (post-CABG), related to chronic lymphedema/venous insufficiency and portal of entry via tinea pedis.
b) Most likely organism: non-group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus (group C, G, or B).
c) Three interventions to reduce recurrence: (1) Treat/prevent interdigital tinea pedis. (2) Compression stockings and limb elevation/skin hygiene to reduce lymphedema (lymphatic pneumatic compression if needed). (3) Prophylactic antibiotics (e.g., monthly benzathine penicillin or oral penicillin V) for patients with frequent recurrences.

cohort_answer.text: A) Larva currens caused by Strongyloidiasis infection. B) Strongyloides serology; Stool O+P (and possibly urine O+P); biopsy of skin lesion for histopathology. C) HTLV-1; HIV (has been reported in AIDS but not to extent expected, not AIDS-defining); any condition requiring steroid therapy associated with hyperinfection. questions.question: Patient post heart transplant with recurrent cellulitis.

parts.text: What is the most common infecting organism?
What are 3 things you can do to try to minimize recurrence?

cohort_answer.text: S. aureus most common (DDx: enterococci, GNB, Candida, M. hominis, rarely mucor/crypto). Minimize recurrence: screening nares for S. aureus decolonization pre-transplant, S. aureus decolonization, antibiotic prophylaxis; foot care (treat cutaneous fungal infections, cuts/bruises); reduce immunosuppression if possible; compression stockings if edema.

questions.question: Homeless man comes to OPAT clinic. He has purulent cellulitis.

parts.text: What are the two organisms most likely to be responsible?
He remembers that he cut his leg on a seashell by the seashore. You want to cover for Vibrio vulnificus. What is the best oral regimen to empirically cover these organisms?
Give two further regimens can be IV or oral. If IV can only be given once per day. If po can only be given twice per day. Can only have two drugs max in each regimen.
Name 5 more organisms that can cause “marine associated” skin/soft tissue infection.

questions.model_answer:
a) Two most likely organisms: Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA) and Streptococcus pyogenes (group A Streptococcus).
b) Best oral empiric regimen to also cover Vibrio vulnificus: doxycycline (active against MRSA, streptococci, and Vibrio vulnificus).
c) Two alternative regimens (IV once daily and/or oral twice daily, maximum two drugs each): Regimen 1 - ceftriaxone 1-2 g IV once daily plus trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole PO twice daily. Regimen 2 - ertapenem 1 g IV once daily plus linezolid 600 mg PO/IV twice daily.
d) Five further marine-associated SSTI organisms: Aeromonas hydrophila, Mycobacterium marinum, Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae, Edwardsiella tarda, and Shewanella putrefaciens.

questions.question: Healthy guy has necrotizing fasciitis of the upper arm

parts.text: How to confirm diagnosis
What is an empiric antibiotic regimen
Gram stain shows gram positive cocci in chains, describe precautions required
Wife has anaphylaxis to Penicillin, list 2 agents from different classes that can be used for post-exposure prophylaxis

cohort_answer.text: Confirm diagnosis: Clinical diagnosis from surgical intervention - rapidly progressive, pain out of proportion, dishwater fluid appearance when fascia is entered surgically. The fascia at time of direct visual examination is swollen and dull gray with stringy areas of necrosis; a thin, brownish exudate may be present. Empiric regimen: Piperacillin-Tazobactam, Vancomycin, Clindamycin. Precautions: Contact and droplet until on appropriate therapy for 24 hours. Post-exposure prophylaxis: Azithromycin 500mg PO daily x5/7; Clindamycin 300mg PO TID x10/7; PCN dosing 250mg PO QID x10/7

questions.question: Unstable patient with clinical picture of necrotizing fasciitis, swab of clinical sample is positive for GPC in chains.

parts.text: Empiric Abx
What are two other treatments that must be considered?
What is the underlying virulence factor
Wife asks whether she is at risk for invasive GAS compared to the general population. What do you tell her?

cohort_answer.text: Empiric: PipTazo + Vanco + Clindamycin (awaiting speciation); once GAS confirmed: Pen G + Clinda. Other treatments: Surgical debridement for source control, IVIG (consider for streptococcal TSS), fluid resuscitation. Virulence factor: M protein (major somatic virulence factor of GAS, antiphagocytic via alternate complement pathway inhibition). Risk to contacts: risk of subsequent invasive GAS disease among household contacts is roughly 20-fold (Mandell's: 66/100,000 vs 3.5/100,000 in general population); some sources cite 200-2000 fold higher risk than general population

questions.question: Organisms associated with soft tissue infection following water exposure

parts.text: Name 5 organisms

cohort_answer.text: Fresh water: Aeromonas hydrophilia, Burkholderia pseudomallei, Streptococcus iniae, Chromobacterium violaceum, Edwardsiella tarda, Plesiomonas shigelloides, Pseudomonas. Salt water: Vibrio vulnificus, Mycobacterium marinum (also fresh), Mycobacterium fortuitum (also fresh), Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae, Shewanella spp. Also Prototheca in immunocompromised.

cohort_answer.text: Pathogens: GAS, S. aureus. Vibrio drug: Ciprofloxacin. Alternative regimens: IV CRO + doxy, or CRO + levofloxacin (can also use ceftazidime as 3rd gen ceph but dosing frequency 3x daily).
